Google does not get to read the source code; it can only decompile/debug a code blob stored inside the APK.
I thought they have some kind of SDK to run and check what's inside. What if somebody puts malicious code? How does it get detected? Are you a developer, do you have some insight overwiews?

Google runs all app submissions through a Bouncer program, which presumably attempts to detect dodgy activity in apps like requiring too many permissions or calling home with lots of user information. They don't review the source code, and even if they did, it would probably be way too complex to find malicious behaviour/bugs with a 100% success rate. OpenSSL is open-source and Heartbleed existed in that for a few years before anybody realised.

They probably have the same or equivalent tools compared to what everyone else has.

I'm not a habitual app developer, though I've done a little research and a little Android app developing.

There are a few way to check malicious code. Remember, it's in compiled form, so it's not in a form that a human could easily read:

  • Decompile it; you won't get a perfect reproduction but you'll have something that's easier to investigate. You should see API calls plainly if you decompile it. Your decompiled code may be read to read because things like variable names are ambiguously referenced in the compiled code. (They're sort-of numbered and may cause trouble because the original names may be descriptive. Perhaps a variable was called "numAttempts" but your decompiler could only present to you "variable2") There are also tools that will obfuscate the original source code which may make the decompiled code difficult to read.

  • Simply look at permissions. That will stop the most basic naughtiness. Why does a flashlight need access to contacts?

  • Monitor network activity

I think the best way to combat this is to destroy the idea of closed-source software and make it normal for developers to be expected to release source code for the world, not just for Google, to share, extend, and audit.

Like the title says, what's one tech related purchase you were initially excited about, possibly even lined up for, but ultimately regretted buying or were just seriously let down with?

For me, it was the Apple Watch. I was thrilled about it simply being a fan of Apple devices. At the end of the day it was the first Apple product I truly felt was a waste of money purely for the sake of being able to say "I have one of those". I realize many people see Apple devices as such across the board, but usually for me they are productive machines and I enjoy them. I expected the watch to be super useful, but at the end of the day it adds steps to the workflow rather than removes them.
What's one tech purchase you were thrilled with but ended up regretting?

So I generally started off very against the Apple watch and my girlfriend essentially has 'Apple watch' hardwired as a trigger word for her to go on an epic rant about how functionally useless it is and how Apple has duped everyone into thinking they've innovated once again.

My boss ended up getting one for the reason that he wanted to improve his health like a Fitbit. He's also a huge Harley buff and the number one useful thing about it is the GPS system for him when riding. A little buzz to let you know you should be turning here etc, but without having to fumble with a phone. It is obviously ridiculously overpriced like all Apple shit, but as more apps are trying to cash in on its existence maybe it'll eventually justify its price tag. I don't believe it will though.

You know, I could see that for bikers or certain other circumstances, but the problem for me is that when it vibrates, it's so weak. I mean, I have to be sitting perfectly still to feel it at all.

My biggest complaints with it:

  1. It just doesn't feel good to work with. It is slightly more convenient to raise your wrist than to slide your phone out of your pocket when you get a notification... however to do anything with the notifications you're going to be getting your phone out anyway, so it works out to be an extra step rather than a time saver.

  2. Price point. I could have seen it for $99-$150 starting, and capping off at about where it is now or no more than $500. There's just not enough uses for it (yet) to justify it. To achieve the things it can do that your phone can't, you could buy a fitness band, a good watch, and still have a good sized chunk of change to play with.

  3. The absolute negatives. Not only do you have to charge the watch daily (which I didn't think at first would bother me, but having it now, it does) but it also deeply affects battery life of your phone. Pairing the watch with my 6 Plus is the first time I've not only not gotten 48 hours out of my 6 Plus between charges, but it was also the first time it didn't make it from 6am-6pm. That makes it effectively useless for me. It works off bluetooth if it's on the same wifi network as your phone, but for some of us who work out of an office, that isn't a viable alternative. They need to get it off needing the phone. Plus, again, you absolutely have to have your phone on you to use it anyway, and there's nothing (outside fitness tracking) that it can do that your phone can't do better or far easier.

You're right though. Maybe as more apps are put out for it or in it's 2nd or 3rd generations (if it makes it there, rather than going the route of iPod Hifi) it will justify it's price tag better.
